newsitem.title: USA: Ecuador, Colombia woes hinder Valentine shipments.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador, Colombia woes hinder Valentine shipments.

text.p: Shippers and air cargo executives were pushing through about the same amount of Valentine's flowers this year as last, despite problems in the two biggest flower exporting countries, industry officials said Tuesday.
"Getting flowers out of Miami is not a problem," Ken Shaw, owner of Miami-based Royal Floral Distributers Inc., said, "It has been getting them into Miami that has been a challenge."
A general strike followed by political turmoil this week in Ecuador made it hard for Royal and others to get their roses from farm to airport.

Royal used a helicopter to ferry the blooms over any possible trouble between the fields and airport in Quito and will continue to use it until the rush is over Tuesday. "Some roads are open but we're not taking any chances," Teodoro Calle, Shaw's partner, said.

Sunburst Farms, the biggest flower importer in Miami, did not resort to local air cargo to get to the airport. "We transported at off-hours and on back roads," Sunburst Vice President William Surplus said.

A government employees strike on Tuesday in Colombia kept many flights from taking off from Bogota and other airports, Guillermo Mejia, Miami-based commercial director for Colombia's all-cargo Tampa Airlines SA, said.
"We have not had any flights today so far," Mejia said. But he said the strike would not disrupt Valentine's Day flower delivery.
"Everyone knew about the strike so they got all of the flowers out Monday night," he said. Tampa normally has six flights per day from Colombia.
Growers complained of much higher cargo rates, partly due to higher fuel costs and partly due to traditional seasonal hikes. "Airlines take advantage this time of year," Calle said.
"The rates from Bogota are double what they were in July," Surplus said.
Surplus also complained of not enough lift out of Ecuador. Millon Air, a Miami-based all cargo airline, has been grounded since an accident in October.
"That has actually been more of a problem than the strike," Surplus said.

Challenge Air Cargo, the Miami-based all-cargo carrier, was running 12,000 to 15,000 boxes of flowers, mostly roses, per day. Challenge Perishables Manager Sylvia Cuesto was expecting five flights full of flowers Monday night. Challenge has been running three daily flights from Bogota and three from Quito, compared with the normal one from Bogota and two from Quito, Cuesta said. Other flower flights come from Costa Rica and Guatamala.
Challenge's 30,000 square foot cooler is "totally full," Cuesto said.
Tuesday flights will have fewer flowers because the flowers will not get to flower shops worldwide by Valentine's Day Friday.

Most flowers that come into the United States and go on to Europe and other destinations come through Miami International Airport. Flowers are MIA's biggest single import commodity with about 167,000 tons passing through in 1995.
Valentine's Day is one of the busiest times, but Mother's Day beats Valentine's in volume.
About $8 billion of cut flowers are sold in the United States yearly, according to the Colombian Flower Council.
